Silence has never been this loud.
ABOUT
A gunshot in occupied territory. A soldier shoots a deaf boy in a public square. The next day, the whole town wakes up deaf, refusing to hear the soldiers, teaching one another a sign language of resistance. From that premise, drawn from Ilya Kaminsky‘s acclaimed poetic narrative, Dublin’s Dead Centre and Sign Language poet Zoë McWhinney build one of the most striking imports of the season: a fable of occupation in which silence becomes both a hiding place and an act of defiance.
A deaf and hearing ensemble lead a production that folds sign language, puppetry, live cinema, and music into a single charged form, turning quiet itself into something political. Fresh from its acclaimed premiere at London’s Royal Court, where it was named as one of
The Stage
‘s top shows of 2025, Deaf Republic is theater of rare invention and rare feeling, holding a whole town’s refusal to listen up against a world that will not stop shouting.

records.title: Discussion with Director of Hungarian documentary on press freedom, “80 Angry Journalists”
records.description:
Short clip then discussion
“80 Angry Journalists” (80 dühös újságíró), about press freedom in Hungary, premieres at DOC NYC on November 12 after a strong run at European festivals. Its director, András Földes, is a journalist and filmmaker, and its lead subject, Vera Munk, is editor-in-chief of 444 and former editor-in-chief of Telex. The film is arguably more timely now, even after April’s elections ended Orbán’s 16 years in power. The media system built over that period, from a captured public broadcaster to consolidated pro-government outlets, does not disappear with a change of government, and the journalists in the film are now navigating that transition. Their experience offers lessons for newsrooms elsewhere facing political pressure, both in resisting it and in rebuilding afterward.

Expanding the Ancient World
is a series of professional development workshops and online resources for teachers. Keyed to the NYC Department of Education Social Studies Scope and Sequence, this program is designed to offer K-12 educators opportunities to develop their knowledge of the ancient world and to provide classroom-ready strategies for teaching the past with reliable sources. Featuring inquiry-based workshops, flexible lesson plans, and up-to-date research, Expanding the Ancient World aims to equip teachers with information and skills that they can share with their students. CTLE credits will be offered to New York State teachers.
Visual art is an invaluable resource for the study of the ancient world. Through visual representations we can assess many aspects of past cultures, from daily life to belief systems, politics, economy, and more. One of the most informative types of art for understanding ancient Greek culture of the Archaic and Classical periods (c. 800–323 BCE) is vase painting. In this workshop, we will examine gender through ancient Greek painted vases, with a focus on vases produced in Attica, first by discussing how and why decorated terracotta vases were produced and how they were used. We will analyze pictorial scenes on ancient Greek painted vases to assess how gender operated in Greek society in the Archaic and Classical periods, touching on traditional and ideal roles, activity, and physical appearance for men and women, as well as mythic and human figures that challenged gendered ideals. Furthermore, we will interrogate how and why we use art as a type of evidence and consider how cultural values and beliefs inform artistic visual representation. The lesson plan from this workshop aims to equip students with skills to critically describe, evaluate, and assess visual primary sources as a tool for understanding the past; to inform them about values, beliefs, and daily life in Greek culture; and to reflect on the importance of individual and group identity within cultures both ancient and modern.

Participants will receive 1.5 CTLE hours.

2026 marks the centenary of the death of Italian journalist, radical liberal, and anti-fascist intellectual Piero Gobetti (1901–26). Today, his insights into liberalism and anti-fascism resonate more than ever, particularly in light of the resurgence of reactionary politics reminiscent of fascism and ongoing debates surrounding (neo-)liberalism.
An Intellectual against Fascism
offers anglophone readers a new translation of over thirty articles that span Gobetti’s entire journalistic career, half of which have previously been unavailable in English. The volume is thoughtfully organized to allow readers to trace the progressive development of his ideas. To enhance understanding of Gobetti’s thought, this expertly curated collection includes his writings on literature, theatre, and literary criticism. It also features the complete text of
La Rivoluzione Liberale
(1924), his magnum opus, which has not been available in its entirety before. An extensive critical apparatus accompanies the collection, including a preface, an introduction, and concise introductions and notes for each article.

records.title: Roundtable: Italian Feminism(s)
records.description:
Click here to RSVP
Roundtable
Italian Feminism(s)
Words and Voices from a Kaleidoscopic Movement
Featuring:
Alessandra Abate
(Ph.D. Candidate, NYU)
on Lea Melandri
Serena Bassi
(Yale University)
on Silvia Federici
Alessandro Giammei
(Yale University)
on Carla Lonzi
Diletta Pasetti
(Rutgers University)
on Gabriella Parca
Vanessa Roghi
(NYU)
on Michela Murgia
Moderated by
Teresa Bertilotti
(Ljubljana University)
In ENGLISH
How many feminisms have crossed Italy?
One distinctive feature of Italian feminism is how personal experience, collective practice, and theoretical reflection have deeply shaped one another, expressing a plurality of perspectives. From the mid-1960s, the movement took shape through various initiatives and often divergent standpoints, from autonomous collectives such as
Rivolta Femminile
, which practiced consciousness-raising, to Marxist feminist groups that demanded wages for housework, as well as campaigns for abortion and divorce rights and early forms of lesbian feminist organizing. These debates over sexuality, unpaid labor, and civil rights raised questions that still inform contemporary feminist politics.
By bringing five figures from different generations and traditions into dialogue–emblems of the many nuances this movement produced–, this roundtable navigates their viewpoints through a conversation rooted in their own words. Starting from their texts, the discussion explores how theorists, activists, writers, and journalists who reflected on body, family, and sexuality drew on their experiences to develop ideas and intervene in public life, raising questions that still resonate today.
Because the personal is always political.

Conventional studies of ancient Jewish prayer and its evolution focus primarily on recitations or performances of precatory texts, liturgy, or poetry once conducted inside Jewish homes, synagogues, and study halls. This talk adopts a different focus: it considers inextricable connections between the minds, hearts, and bodies of Jewish supplicants and the portable things that they once attached to their bodies with strings and cords, including inscribed amulets and phylacteries of various sorts. Through explorations of objects from ISAW’s exhibition
Cursed! The Power of Magic in the Ancient World
, as well as those found in other museum exhibitions and collections, this lecture examines haptic and material dimensions of Jewish prayer, as facilitated through attention to wearable objects that originally encased hidden texts. Drawing additional insights from recent studies of ancient magic and ritual power throughout Egyptian, Greek, Roman, and Mesopotamian cultural orbits, as well as neglected archaeological discoveries from synagogue contexts, the lecture offers novel insights into relationships between amulets and phylacteries, Jewish prayer, and the complex “marketplace” of religions throughout the ancient world.
Karen B. Stern (PhD Brown University, 2006) is an award-winning author and professor at Brooklyn College and the Graduate Center of the City University of New York. Her research synthesizes studies of archaeology, art, and graffiti to reimagine the cultural histories, material cultures, and sensory experiences of Jews and their neighbors throughout the ancient Mediterranean world. She is author of
Writing on the Wall: Graffiti and the Forgotten Jews of Antiquity
(Princeton University Press 2018; paperback ed. 2020), winner of a 2020 Jordan Schnitzer Book Award;
Inscribing Devotion and Death: Archaeological Evidence for Jewish Populations of North Africa
(Brill 2008); and co-editor of
With the Loyal You Show Yourself Loyal: Essays on Relationships in the Hebrew Bible in Honor of Saul M. Olyan
(SBL Press 2021). Research grants, fellowships, and residencies from the Guggenheim Foundation, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Council of American Overseas Research Centers, the Getty Villa, the Center for Jewish History, and others have supported her academic and field research. Her current book project, ‘Sacred: Archaeology of the Senses in the Ancient Synagogue,’ investigates experiential and multi-sensory dimensions of Jewish devotional life in antiquity.

Join former FDNY Commissioner and NYU Wagner Researcher-in-Residence Laura Kavanagh and Melanie E. La Rocca (Chief Operating Officer, RiseBoro Community Partnership & former Commissioner, NYCDOB) for a fireside chat to discuss how fire departments and housing agencies can work together to keep New Yorkers safe while building the homes the city needs.
Our building and fire codes exist to protect residents. But as New York works to expand housing through building and renovation, a key question is whether those codes weigh risk in the right way. records.description:
James Osborne
University of Chicago
Since the 2019 discovery of a royal inscription authored by “Great King Hartapu,” Iron Age Anatolian scholarship has been energised by the appearance of a hitherto unknown kingdom in the Konya Plain. While the historical context of Hartapu’s inscriptions have undergone dramatic reassessment in light of this new text, little attention has been paid to the conditions that would have contributed to the rise of this kingdom in the first place. This lecture proposes several factors that likely played a role in the emergence of the kingdom: cultural and economic interaction with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, similar relations with Phrygia, emulative competition with its local peer polities and a propitious ecological setting at a time of significant environmental transformations.
This lecture will take place in person at
ISAW
(15 East 84th Street).
Registration is required. Please fill out the form at the bottom of this page.
This talk is cosponsored by ISAW and the Archaeological Institute of America-New York Society.
Abstract
Since the 2019 discovery of a royal inscription authored by “Great King Hartapu,” Iron Age Anatolian scholarship has been energised by the appearance of a hitherto unknown kingdom in the Konya Plain. While the historical context of Hartapu’s inscriptions have undergone dramatic reassessment in light of this new text, little attention has been paid to the conditions that would have contributed to the rise of this kingdom in the first place. This lecture proposes several factors that likely played a role in the emergence of the kingdom: cultural and economic interaction with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, similar relations with Phrygia, emulative competition with its local peer polities and a propitious ecological setting at a time of significant environmental transformations. Results from newly launched excavations at Türkmen-Karahöyük, almost certainly Hartapu’s capital city, help illustrate these points. Interspersed with these arguments are reflections and anecdotes about Hartapu, and especially the way we represent Hartapu visually, that evoke how the effort we have spent on understanding political dynamics in Hartapu’s kingdom has been imbalanced toward the man himself, with insufficient consideration having been given to longer term, structural forces. Such reflections lead us to reconsider the disproportionately impactful effect of Hartapu’s monuments in the past and the present alike, and the extent to which Hartapu’s kingdom in fact consisted of his own self-imaging.
About the speaker
James Osborne is Associate Professor at the University of Chicago’s Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures. He is a Bronze and Iron Age archaeologist concentrating especially on Anatolia and the Levant during the late second and early first millennium BCE. His monograph
The Syro-Anatolian City-States: An Iron Age Culture
, published by Oxford University Press, was the 2023 winner of the American Schools of Overseas Research’s G. Ernest Wright Award for most substantial book in the archaeology of the Near East and eastern Mediterranean. With Michele Rüzgar Massa (Bilkent University), he is Co-Director of the Türkmen-Karahöyük Archaeological Project.

The Catacombs,
